title: Al-Ghazali's Revival
hookLine: forty books on worship, habits, what destroys and what saves

lines: A BOOK WITH A BOLD TITLE.
cards: A celebrated professor stands up to lecture in Baghdad, and nothing comes out. His tongue won't move. That's how Abu Hamid al-Ghazali tells it, in his own account of his life, called Deliverance from Error.
He held a celebrated teaching post, and he had come to doubt that his learning was doing his soul any good. So he left the post, the students, the reputation, and went traveling.
Out of that turn came a huge book with a bold title.

teach.b: The book is Ihya Ulum al-Din, the Revival of the Religious Sciences. Revival means bringing back to life.
Al-Ghazali's claim was that religious knowledge had grown dry: people knew the rules and argued the fine points, and the heart was left out. So he set out to put it back in.

His introduction gives the plan: four quarters, ten books in each. The first quarter is worship, with books among them on knowledge, belief, purity, prayer, charity, fasting, pilgrimage, the Qur'an, remembrance.
The second is everyday life, the habits: eating, marriage, earning a living, friendship, travel. Then the turn inward.

The third quarter is what destroys: the heart's diseases, like anger, envy, greed, showing off, pride. And the fourth is what saves: the heart's cures, like repentance, patience, gratitude, hope, love. Notice the order.

You don't reach the soul's inner rooms by skipping the kitchen and the marketplace. Ordinary life comes first; then the doctor examines the heart, sickness before cure. That's why this block keeps coming back to him.

teach.h: A DOCTOR'S MANUAL FOR THE HEART.
teach.b: His book reads like a doctor's manual: here is a vice, here is how it grows, here is how it's treated. The cures he names become the stations of the coming days.
And the Revival treats a bad temper the way you'd treat a sprained ankle: seriously, step by step, without shame, expecting it can heal.

how: Students of the inward path read al-Ghazali's Ihya Ulum al-Din, the Revival of the Religious Sciences, sometimes book by book with a teacher.

o: a reform movement that swept Baghdad's mosques in his day
al-Ghazali's book for bringing the heart back into religion
a yearly festival that renews faith after Ramadan ends

s: the Revival begins with the heart's diseases
it begins with worship, then everyday habits, and only then turns inward.
al-Ghazali describes leaving his teaching post after a crisis
in Deliverance from Error he tells of being unable to lecture, and leaving.
the Revival treats vices as things that can be treated, like an illness
it reads like a doctor's manual: the vice, how it grows, how it heals.

games.q: you're al-Ghazali, at the top of your field in Baghdad, and you doubt your learning is helping your soul. what do you do?
o: keep lecturing and push the doubt down.
leave the post and go traveling.
write a book refuting your doubts.
games.why: in his own account, he left the post and the reputation, and the Revival grew out of that turn.

practice: Here are a few books of the Revival: The Book of Knowledge, of the Etiquette of Eating, of the Marvels of the Heart, of the Dangers of the Tongue, of Repentance, of Patience and Gratitude.

Let the one that tugs a little choose you, and sit with the question: what would a chapter on this say about my life? If you pray, ask Allah for beneficial knowledge; if not, let the title rest in you.

wordCard.voice: Al-Ghazali's Revival. The Ihya: a great work in four quarters, worship, habits, what destroys and what saves, written to bring the heart back into religious knowledge. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the revival of the sciences of the religion.

carryVoice: Your line: the revival. Every ordinary habit, eating, speaking, working, shapes the heart. See you tomorrow.
